Clear mandates and interoperable frameworks are also necessary to avoid overlapping authority and institutional silos, especially in federated governance systems.

Questions of data ownership — particularly when involving private-sector generated data (e.g., smart meter data, grid usage patterns) — must be addressed through both legal clarity and operational protocols.

Countries such as Estonia and Finland have experimented with data embassies and cross-border data exchange frameworks that ensure sovereignty and access rights while allowing secure, compliant sharing of information.
A Whole-of-Government Approach
Finally, a whole-of-government approach to digital transformation is crucial.
This means not only investing in technical skills and platforms, but also creating leadership structures that empower innovation and ensure accountability.

Independent data stewardship bodies, open standards, and data trusts may offer pathways to ethically and efficiently manage energy data, enabling AI-driven solutions without compromising privacy or public interest.
Public Data Commons
Finally, public data commons, which are public sites where cleaned and standardized datasets related to energy can be accessed, incentivize innovation.

Trough the availability of this data in a free, open access platform, barriers to entry for startups and researchers are lowered, private public partnerships are encouraged, and trust is built, as data shared is usually accompanied by metadata.
Key examples of such initiatives are the Stanford School of Sustainability’s Data Commons for Climate, Energy, and Sustainability and the US government’s Open Energy Data Initiative.
Metadata

In addition, metadata, also known as the “data about data” provides valuable, trust-building information about the data being shared, including the units in which the data is expressed, who collected it, when it was collected, as well as the format of the file.
This information allows analysts to trust the data, while also enhancing interoperability, whereby systems can use, reuse and integrate the data into their daily operations.

Given the growing need for standardization, multiple world organizations have started adopting the Statistical Data and Metadata eXchange, or SDMX, which is a set of internationally recognized standards, which make it easier to publish and exchange data in an understandable way.

Key parts of a Smart Grid
Advanced Metering (AMI)
Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) is the set of equipment and systems that have been developed over the last few years to allow the intelligence management of the end-user distribution network.
Smart meters, which enable two-way communication between customers and the utility company, are a feature of smart grids.
These meters periodically capture data on power consumption, allowing consumers to manage their energy use and supporting dynamic pricing schemes.
Control and Automation of the Grid
In a smart grid, automation is important.
It optimizes electricity flow, detects faults, and monitors grid performance using sophisticated algorithms and control systems.
The system can react fast, frequently even before users notice, when a problem is identified, such as a power outage or voltage fluctuation.
Integration of Renewable Energy
Smart grids play a pivotal role in integrating renewable energy sources by leveraging real-time data and advanced technologies to address the intermittency challenges of renewables.
Smart meters, for instance, enable demand-side responses and time-of-use pricing, helping to balance energy loads more effectively.
While these tools are not the ultimate solution, they support the overarching goal of creating a more flexible and adaptive grid.
By dynamically managing energy flows and coordinating diverse energy sources, smart grids ensure a reliable and stable energy supply, even as the share of variable renewable energy continues to grow.
Programs for Demand Response
Demand response programs in smart grids empower consumers to take an active role in managing their energy consumption.
Through time-of-use pricing, customers are incentivized to reduce their usage or shift it to off-peak hours when electricity demand is lower and prices are more affordable.

This not only helps consumers save on energy costs but also supports grid stability by alleviating pressure during peak demand periods, contributing to more efficient load control and a more reliable energy system.
Advanced grid management techniques are essential for effectively integrating renewable energy projects into the electrical grid.
They help optimize energy production, distribution, and consumption while ensuring grid stability.
It involves deploying cutting-edge technologies, systems, and strategies to enhance the reliability, resilience, efficiency, and sustainability of the electric grid.
Real-Time Monitoring
Constant data gathering and analysis of grid characteristics, such as voltage, current, frequency, and grid congestion, constitute real-time monitoring.
Current data on the state of the grid is provided by sophisticated sensors and communication networks.
Managing the unpredictability of renewable energy sources requires real-time monitoring.

To maintain grid stability and make effective use of renewable energy, grid operators can make real-time adjustments to configurations and resource allocations depending on actual generation and consumption.
Demand Response (DR)
Demand response is a technique that involves adjusting energy consumption in reaction to price signals, grid conditions, or other factors.
It enables users to choose to adjust or decrease their electricity use at times of peak demand or in reaction to rising electricity costs.
By lowering peak load and coordinating energy use with the patterns of renewable energy generation, demand response helps maintain grid balance.

Demand response programs, for example, can encourage users to use more electricity or store extra energy during times of strong solar or wind generation, which lessens the need for fossil fuel-based power plants during peak demand.

Distribution Automation
Distribution automation uses advanced control systems and sensors to manage the electricity grid more effectively.
Think of it as a smart system that can detect problems, switch off damaged parts of the grid, and even fix itself in some cases.
This makes the grid more reliable and able to handle renewable energy sources, like solar and wind, which can be more unpredictable.
When combined with real-time monitoring, it can quickly find and isolate issues, minimizing power outages and making sure the grid runs smoothly and efficiently.
This technology helps keep the lights on even when things go wrong, improving the overall stability of the energy system.
Advanced Grid Analytics

To forecast grid conditions, evaluate data from multiple sources, and make well-informed judgements for grid management, advanced grid analytics leverages data analytics and machine learning algorithms.
By using these analytics to forecast demand trends, renewable energy output, and grid conditions, grid operators can take proactive measures to maintain the grid.
Optimizing the integration of renewable energy is made possible by predictive analytics, which offers insights into energy storage, dispatch tactics, and grid capacity planning.
Grid-Connected Energy Storage
The idea behind these systems is that they store extra energy during times when renewable energy production is at its peak and release it when required.
Examples of these systems include batteries.
Energy storage devices are essential for maintaining a balance between supply and demand.
By storing excess renewable energy and releasing it during periods of low generation, they maintain grid stability and lessen the need for backup fossil fuel power.
Case Study RBEC: UNDP Moldova contributes to the digitalization of the energy system by building a smart grid
Over the past two years, the Republic of Moldova has emerged as the nation most impacted by the energy crisis, second only to Ukraine.
In the previous year, more than 60% of Moldovan households spent over 10% of their family income on energy, leading to widespread energy poverty.
Coupled with an inflation rate exceeding 30%, these factors have driven more than a quarter of the population into poverty, surviving on less than US$1.50 per day [1].
Mitigating energy poverty in RBEC via digitalization is one of the priorities of UNDP in the region.

A project implemented in Moldova by UNDP in partnership with the Ministry of Energy with the financial support of the Italian Government is a successful example to showcase an installation of smart meters for Moldovan citizens, with a particular attention to suburban population.

As energy poverty is one of the main issues in the region, this project targeted specific groups of households and selected them based on the following criteria: of geographical location, population density, energy vulnerability, socio-economic status, and availability of infrastructure [2].
The main objective of the project is to digitalize the energy sector in Moldova by implementing smart grid technology, which includes the installation of smart meters.

This aims to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of energy consumption measurement, improve energy management, integrate renewable energy sources, reduce operational costs, and enable time-of-use differentiated tariffs for consumers.

Ultimately, the project seeks to foster more efficient energy use, reduce energy dependency, and lower greenhouse gas emissions.
Smart meters will provide real-time data on consumption and energy quality, allowing for automatic and secure transmission of information to energy suppliers.
This eliminates the need for manual meter readings, enables accurate billing based on actual consumption, and helps quickly identify and respond to power outages.
With support from the EU, UNDP implemented a behavioral experiment targeting households with above-average energy consumption.
These households received letters informing them about their high energy use and providing tips for saving energy.
In 2022, over 140,000 households in northern Moldova, serviced by FEE Nord, received these letters.
The aim was to see if such letters would lead to reduced energy consumption, independent of electricity price increases.
The results showed that households receiving the letters reduced their consumption by up to 22%.
Households using more than 200kWh per month were the most responsive, reducing consumption significantly, while those using less were less impacted, saving between 2-8%.
The most substantial impact was seen in the first three months, with reductions of 10-20%, which then fell below 10% or stabilized in subsequent months [1].
In 2023, the Fund launched an online platform as an innovative solution to combat energy crisis.
"Rabla for Household Appliances" helps vulnerable families reduce electricity bills by replacing old appliances with energy-efficient ones.
The first stage started in November 2023, and it offered free LED bulb vouchers to around 50,000 families.
Vouchers will go to those registered last year in the Energy Vulnerability Information System on compensatii.gov.md, categorized as very high energy vulnerability.
Priority is given to families with children, based on the number of children and their electricity consumption.
Beneficiaries were notified via SMS, email, or phone about voucher availability in their compensatii.gov.md accounts.
Those without mobile phones or internet access received assistance from the Unified Centers for the Provision of Public Services (CUPS) [4].

Part 3: A.I.
in energy forecasting and demand prediction
Accurate energy forecasts are crucial for effective energy planning, as they enable energy providers to anticipate future demand and ensure a reliable energy supply.
Energy forecasting refers to the process of predicting future energy consumption or production based on historical data, weather patterns, economic trends, and other influencing factors.

In this context, what is being forecasted is the future demand for energy, which includes understanding peak consumption times, seasonal fluctuations, and the integration of renewable energy sources that can be intermittent.
Precise energy forecasts help optimize the operation of power plants, reduce operational costs, and minimize environmental impact by balancing supply and demand efficiently.

Machine learning algorithms, such as neural networks, support vector machines, and ensemble learning methods, analyze historical data and identify complex patterns that traditional statistical methods might miss, enabling more accurate predictions and smarter decision-making .

One of the pioneering applications of A.I.
in energy prediction is Google’s A.I.
subsidiary, DeepMind.
DeepMind created a machine learning algorithm capable of predicting wind farm productivity, i.e., forecasting wind power, up to 36 hours in advance.

By training a neural network on accessible weather forecasts and historical turbine data, DeepMind's system forecasts wind power output and advises on optimal hourly delivery commitments to the power grid a day ahead.
This system supports 700MW of wind capacity for powering the company's data centers and offices in the US.
It enabled Google to sell wind power supply in advance, increasing its financial value by 20% by early 2019 .
Other notable examples are two AI-powered applications developed by ABB in collaboration with Verdigris Technologies, designed to improve energy management in commercial and industrial buildings.
The first application, ‘Energy Forecasting,’ uses machine learning algorithms to predict future energy consumption and help businesses manage peak demand, ultimately reducing electricity bills.
The second application, ‘Intelligent Alerts,’ leverages AI to continuously monitor critical assets, detecting potential issues before they cause disruptions to energy supply.
These applications are part of ABB's Open Innovation program, which focuses on digital transformation by providing advanced tools for better energy management and cost reduction .

Together, these innovations highlight the potential of AI to optimize energy usage, lower operational costs, and improve the reliability and sustainability of energy systems.

The integration of A.I.
and data science in the energy sector has revolutionized predictive maintenance, grid management, and energy forecasting.
Advanced machine learning algorithms enable proactive maintenance, enhance operational efficiency, and ensure reliable energy networks.
A.I.-driven grid management improves stability and integration of renewable energy sources, while advanced forecasting optimizes resource usage, and reduces costs.
These advances demonstrate the profound impact of A.I.
in creating a more efficient, resilient, and sustainable energy sector.

Part 4: Expanding AI Applications in the Energy Sector
The global energy sector is faced with the critical task of transitioning from fossil fuels to clean, sustainable energy sources to mitigate climate change.
A.I.
has emerged as a powerful tool with the potential to significantly accelerate this transition and achieve ambitious sustainability goals.
While A.I.'s impacts include both positive and negative aspects, the benefits generally outweigh the drawbacks.
A.I.
can predict renewable energy generation and optimize grid operations to integrate these sources more effectively, leading to a more reliable and resilient power grid.
This minimizes the need for backup fossil fuel generation and paves the way for a larger share of renewables in the energy mix.
Furthermore, A.I.
can analyze vast amounts of data to pinpoint the biggest sources of carbon emissions, guiding targeted efforts to reduce them and playing a crucial role in achieving net-zero emissions goals.
Additionally, A.I.

can assist in developing and deploying carbon capture and storage technologies, which are critical components of decarbonization.

According to a report by BloombergNEF (BNEF) released by the World Economic Forum, A.I.
has potential to generate significant value for the global energy transition.
BNEF’s net-zero scenario modelling indicates that each 1% increase in efficiency in energy demand could result in $1.3 trillion in value from 2020 to 2050 by decreasing the need for investment.
Implementing A.I.

in the energy sector could realize these gains by enhancing energy efficiency and adjusting demand .

Despite legitimate concerns about data privacy, security in energy systems, and potential biases, the benefits of A.I.
in the energy sector are evident and substantial.

for energy efficiency in buildings, transport and industry
A.I.
has the potential to significantly improve energy efficiency in a variety of applications.
In buildings and smart homes, internet of things (IoT) devices and smart meters can integrate with A.I.
to build responsive, intelligent ecosystems.
These systems provide real-time, continuous monitoring of energy consumption, for example, which enables A.I.

to make data-driven decisions that maximize energy efficiency.

A.I.
also can be employed to optimize heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems, which are significant contributors to energy consumption in buildings.
By analyzing data from various sensors, A.I.
can adjust HVAC in real-time based on factors like occupancy, weather conditions, and user preferences.
This not only ensures optimal comfort but also reduces energy wastage.
For example, A.I.
algorithms can predict peak usage times and adjust the HVAC system accordingly to maintain efficiency and comfort while minimizing energy use .

This technology has already been implemented in two apartment buildings in Sweden, resulting in a 20% reduction in energy consumption and improved tenant comfort.

In the transport sector, A.I.
optimizes energy efficiency through fleet management and smart traffic systems.
A.I.
algorithms analyze data from vehicle fleets to optimize routes, reduce fuel consumption, and improve maintenance schedules, which lowers operational costs and reduces environmental impact.

A.I.-powered traffic management systems also adjust traffic signals in real-time based on current traffic conditions, thereby reducing congestion, lowering fuel consumption, and decreasing emissions .

In industries, A.I.
significantly enhances energy efficiency by continuously monitoring and adjusting industrial processes.
This involves analyzing production data to reduce energy consumption and waste, leading to improved production rates and lower operational costs.
Moreover, A.I.
improves production and supply chains by optimizing maintenance cycles, ensuring equipment longevity and operational efficiency24.

By using machine learning algorithms to predict changes in CO₂ emissions and environmental conditions, A.I.

Lesson 1 Overview
Although advances in smart meters, AI, energy management, and prove promising for future generations.
Sustained and sustainable innovations in energy systems, the way energy data is leveraged, and the way in which insights are utilized depend on there being an environment conducive to innovation.

Firstly, a resilient digital infrastructure, which is able to store energy data, and provide computing power for algorithms, whether through localized data centers or through cloud storage and computing platforms is essential as a playground for experimentation.

Furthermore, access to data and research, through collaborative academic research or through public data commons incentivizes participation in energy data initiatives.
On a more regional and global scale, interoperability of systems, which facilitates the sharing of useful data across platforms, may prove essential for the creation of seamless applications.

In addition, the increased adoption of metadata (which provide valuable context on how data was collected and how variables are measured) ensures transparency in data sharing, and allows researchers to fully trust the data at their disposal.

Finally, given the surge in data science applications, as well as the quick adoption of ML algorithms in impactful policy, it becomes more crucial than ever to have personnel that are trained in data science, whether in the civil service, in development work, or in the energy industry specifically.

This effort should come in hand with the creation and adoption of complete data governance strategies and frameworks, while also designing a clear model for data ownership and privacy, defining consent in credible legal terms, adding to the increased international legislation around data in economic partnership agreements.

Part1: Building Digital Infrastructure for Energy Data Platforms, storage, cloud-based architecture, public data commons
The Cloud
A resilient and reliable digital infrastructure is foundational in leveraging data for energy policy.
One facet in the effort towards reliable and democratized access to storage and computing power is the increased use of cloud platforms.
Cloud platforms allow users to gain access to storage and computing power on a virtual machine stored in a remote serve.
On one end, this allows the user to access their data and run their models from anywhere, as they are not physically tied to the physical server.
On the other hand, it allows businesses that do not have access to the capital required to build a physical data center to use this pay-as-you-go service.
Finally, through the Internet of Things, real time measurements and adjustments can be done to energy grids and renewable energy projects.
Digital Infrastructure
Cloud in Practice
An example of this is Gamesa Siemens’s use of drones and Hermes, a digital tool.
Gamesa Siemens is a global wind power provider, and as such must routinely check wind turbines for required maintenance.
Through integration within Microsoft Azure (a cloud platform) and the use, they are able to send photos of wind turbines and store them in the cloud.

In addition, through leveraging of cloud computing, they are able to determine which turbines require maintenance, sifting through large volumes of data which previously would have required hard drives and immense computing resources.
Edge and Fog Computing
Furthermore, for applications that require real time decision making, edge computing-which is when computing and storage is done at or near the source of data generation- offer a unique solution.
A simple example is a smart solar inverter which automatically decides when to send power back into the grid.
For applications where coordination is required, fog computing is increasingly being adopted.
Fog computing allows for an intermediate layer between the cloud and edge devices, perfect for tasks such as coordinating energy supply taking pricing into account and retaining low latency.
The Environmental Cost of Data
Increases in Energy Demand
However, the increased adoption of such data-heavy methodologies comes at an environmental cost.

The increase in demand for infrastructure capable of storing such volumes of data, as well as the computing power necessary to perform these complex calculations is currently driving the demand for energy to new heights.
In Belgium alone, the energy demand from data centers is estimated to go up to anywhere between a whopping 10.5TWh to 34TWh in 2050, from a starting point of 3TWh today.
This raises actual concerns regarding the source used to supply this increase in demand, with some regions resorting back to fossil fuels.
The IEA projects that the worldwide energy demand related to data centers will double to 945TWh by 2030.
Innovation based solutions
However, all is not lost, modern innovation efforts have been focused on rendering data centers more energy efficient.
A way to achieve this is through the use of unconventional materials in the manufacturing of data centers.

Interoperability
Introduction

With the increased availability data, as well as the wealth of methods of processing and extracting insights from data, several ways to ensure the smooth and seamless flow of data have been engineered.
Interoperability
Interoperability, now more than ever, has become crucial.
Interoperability refers to the ability of computer systems and software to exchange and make use of data.

Within the context of energy systems, with multiple moving parts such as smart meters, renewable energy systems, substations and the utility grid, the ability to seamlessly share and use data is essential in the ability to make quick decisions.
Furthermore, the reliability of data is key in making sure inequalities are not perpetuated by energy systems.

Part 3:Institutional Capacity and Data Governance Public sector capabilities, mandates, ownership models, Sandboxes
Overview

Now more than ever, with the growing availability, accessibility and demand for data and data-backed policies, it becomes imperative to have policymakers and civil servants that are knowledgeable in AI and its applications in the energy sector, while also clarifying the rules within which data can be extracted, to which extent it can be used, and to which entities they can be shared.
As such, key questions arise, namely related to who owns energy data, and which agencies should have access to sensitive data.
A Digital Gap in Public Policy

Firstly, given the radical and fast-paced nature of the changes brought on by the digital revolution, a “digital gap” appears in the public sector, whereby infrastructure needs to be revamped, personnel need to be upskilled.

These initiatives require intentional government effort and expenditure, an example of this intention is the UK’s Government Digital Services Academy, which trained 10 000 civil servants between 2014 and 2019.
However, more often than not, it is not the lack of skill in the public sector, but the migration of talent due to the culture within government work.
Indeed, a UK National Audit Service survey found that upskilled personnel tended to leave the civil service less than two years after gaining this new skillset.
This signals a larger issue to do with the culture and framing of innovation within the government.
This indicates a need for effective change management, and encouraging a culture of controlled risk taking.
Regulatory Sandboxes
In this context, regulatory sandboxes and institutional experimentation can serve as valuable tools for building the state's adaptive capacity while also mitigating risks.
Sandboxes, (i.e.

controlled environments where innovations can be tested before being fully deployed) allow governments to pilot new data governance models, AI applications in energy forecasting or efficiency, and alternative ownership frameworks.
These environments can support cross-sector collaboration between regulators, utilities, and technology providers, thereby strengthening institutional learning loops.
